title: How do we multiply decimals by the rule?
description: Five point eight times one point two four is found by taking away the points, multiplying the whole numbers and counting the digits after the point. The answer is then checked with fractions. Keeko doubts that the product is seventy one point nine two.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiply as whole numbers, then put the point so that the product has as many digits after it as the two numbers together. Watch for students who count the digits of only one number.

source: Find 5.8 × 1.24 by the rule, and verify with fractions.
video_script.why: The child has seen that the digits after the point in a product are those of the two numbers added, and now uses it as a rule and checks it with fractions.
video_script.substitution: the book's five point eight times one point two four
video_script.anchor: Five point eight times one point two four, to be found by the rule and checked with fractions
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip counts only the two digits after the point in one point two four and leaves out the one digit in five point eight. The point goes after two places in seven thousand one hundred and ninety two, which gives seventy one point nine two, far above the size check of about seven.
maths_rules: remove the points: 5.8 becomes 58 and 1.24 becomes 124, and 58 × 124 = 7192
digits after the point: 5.8 has 1, 1.24 has 2, so the product has 1 + 2 = 3
the slip: 7192 with two places is 71.92, counting only the places of 1.24
video_script.design: One idea: the whole number product is a thousand times too big, so the point goes three places from the right. Assumes the writing of a decimal as a fraction. Wrong idea: counting the places of one number only. The product stays all video; the decimal appears only on the answer beat.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, count the digits after the point. Five point eight has one, and one point two four has two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One plus two is three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The product has three digits after the point, counted from the right.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, verify with fractions. Five point eight is fifty eight over ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One point two four is one hundred and twenty four over one hundred. Multiply the tops, and multiply the bottoms.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>This gives seven thousand one hundred and ninety two over one thousand.

beats.on_screen: Check: about 6 × 1.2 = 7.2, so the product should be near 7

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check the size. Five point eight is near six, and one point two four is near one point two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six times one point two is seven point two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The product must be close to seven.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Over one thousand, the top becomes seven point one nine two, with three digits after the point.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Five point eight times one point two four is seven point one nine two.
